On the march the column stretches out long, the players at the back cannot see the front, and what carries is the low frequency of the big drum through the crowd. The turns are led by the drum too: the drummer changes where the accents fall and the brass changes section with him. Tempo is stretched a long way — the same band can play very slowly at a funeral and extremely fast at a wedding, and the flexibility in between is controlled by the drummer and the lead trumpeter with looks and body movements.

Brass players use circular breathing or steal a breath while someone else leads; the tuba's long notes need a steady air stream, so its phrases are usually longer and fewer than the trumpet's. The whole band's arranging therefore has a breathing curve: a loud passage is followed by a sparser one held by the bass and the drums, letting the high voices recover before the next wave.

The taraf is mostly strings, its bass announces the harmony half a beat early, and the melody holds its conversation in slides and ornament; Balkan brass cuts its seven- and nine-beat groups with the big drum and the snare, the brass lines up on the head of each group, and the tuba gives the beat almost without stopping. One leans on the drum's accents, the other on the offset between bass and melody.

To be heard from both ends the drummer makes the accents simpler and lower than indoors, and the tuba gives the beat almost without stopping; the complicated ornament is kept for playing on the spot. The band switches between this marching version and the standing version several times in one afternoon.

Its rhythms are often not four against four but groups of unequal length — seven, nine, eleven beats — and the dancers step to the same set of numbers.

Take a seven-beat pattern: it is usually heard as three plus two plus two, or two plus two plus three. Dancers and players share the same grouping, so the same seven beats can be danced two ways. When the band plays, the big drum puts an accent on the head of each group, and the ends of the trumpet phrases often line up with those heads, so melody, drum and steps stick to the same grouping.

這個編制的工作場合是生命禮儀與地方慶典：婚禮、洗禮、成年禮、聖人節、市集開幕、選: This line-up works at rites of passage and local festivals: weddings, baptisms, coming-of-age ceremonies, saints' days, market openings, election rallies and funerals. The wedding use is the fullest — the band goes to the groom's house, walks with the party to the church and then on to the feast, playing different repertoire and tempo the whole way. A funeral is the opposite: slow, drawn in, the brass in its low register with long notes.

The brass divides into three bands — high melody, middle harmony, bass — and the big drum and snare supply not just the beat but a set of accents set against the melody. The band usually plays standing or walking, and a wedding party plays as it walks.

At one tempo, three plus two plus two and two plus two plus three sound completely different; and faster pieces can split each beat in two again, so that a cycle of eleven beats sounds like continuous rolling. The players do not line up through a conductor but through the drum's accents and the fixed closing figures of the melody — everyone is counting the same set of numbers.

The tuba replaced the string bass, the big drum replaced the drum kit, and so the same dance tunes could be played on brass at great volume, suited to open air and to marching.
